records.name: Tumour-associated antigen (TAA)
records.tldr: A tumour-associated antigen is a target that is common in a tumour but can also be present in healthy tissue. A treatment aimed at it can affect both, and can also react with a different, look-alike target.
records.summary:
Many tumour-associated antigens come from unmutated proteins, so their usefulness depends on higher expression, an unusual expression pattern or accessibility in the cancer. A neoantigen, by contrast, arises from a tumour-specific sequence alteration. For an antibody or a chimeric antigen receptor, the question is accessible surface antigen on tumour and on healthy cells. For a peptide-directed T-cell receptor it is the particular peptide displayed by a particular HLA allele. RNA for the source gene establishes neither recognition surface, and a gene-expression result does not specify accessibility or peptide display.

Two hazards need different controls. On-target, off-tumour recognition means the receptor recognises its intended target in the wrong tissue. Off-target cross-reactivity means the receptor also recognises a different molecular target, so screening the intended antigen alone cannot rule it out. A published example of the second is an affinity-enhanced T-cell receptor directed at HLA-A*01-restricted MAGE-A3: in a clinical study the first two treated patients developed cardiogenic shock and died within days, no MAGE-A3 expression was detected in heart tissue at autopsy, and the T cells recognised an unrelated peptide from the striated-muscle protein titin (Linette et al., 2013; Cameron et al., 2013, who describe the preclinical analysis as having found no off-target concern). That illustrates the hazard for one engineered receptor and is not a toxicity rate for tumour-associated targets. Immune tolerance also shapes the available response to self antigens, and a stronger receptor does not remove the need to test healthy tissues and alternative targets.

A shared antigen can support a treatment intended for more than one person's cancer, with a trade-off between tumour coverage and healthy-tissue exposure; expression prevalence in a cohort is not a safe recognition threshold for a product. For vaccine-elicited peptide-specific T cells, a shared antigen offers another candidate when credible private targets are few, which is a coverage hypothesis, not demonstrated benefit. A peptide from a shared antigen and one from a neoantigen may depend on the same HLA allele, so changing the antigen does not restore a missing display route: Tran et al. (2016) documented escape after loss of the restricting HLA allele in one colorectal cancer patient. Antibodies and CARs have different recognition requirements, and epitope spreading is a separate widening of recognition that adding a shared antigen does not guarantee.

notes: The existing antigen record already lists tumour-associated antigen as an alias; this record carries the safety distinctions and uses different aliases.
Fictional X/Y examples in the teaching source were not carried over. Abstract-depth reads on 9 November 2026.

NY-ESO-1 illustrates a shared cancer-testis antigen, rather than a private mutation. Ademuyiwa and colleagues reported immunohistochemical expression in 16% of 168 triple-negative breast cancers and 2% of 47 ER-positive/HER2-negative comparators; the comparison groups had different sampling characteristics, and staining was heterogeneous. Their background describes normal expression restricted to testis. Expression prevalence is neither proof of a displayed peptide on every tumour cell nor evidence that a receptor or vaccine is effective or safe. A shared peptide-directed product still requires the appropriate HLA and functional testing.

Viral proteins provide another possible source of non-self targets, distinct from an altered human protein. NCI identifies HPV as a cause of cervical and oropharyngeal cancers, among other sites. For a proposed viral peptide target, establish viral-protein expression in the relevant cells, compatible peptide-HLA display and receptor recognition. A breast-cancer subtype label alone supplies none of that evidence; it does not establish a viral target or predict benefit from targeting it.

The germ-cell HLA qualification is about a measured recognition surface, not all cells in the testis. Guillaudeux and colleagues purified human pachytene spermatocytes and round spermatids and found low levels of class I HLA transcripts, but detected neither surface nor intracellular HLA-I heavy-chain protein with the antibodies used. This supports limited classical HLA-I display in those examined germ-cell populations, despite transcription. It does not establish absence of every HLA molecule in every testicular cell or condition, and it does not by itself prove that a peptide-directed engineered receptor is safe.

records.name: On-target, off-tumour toxicity and off-target cross-reactivity
records.tldr: On-target, off-tumour toxicity is harm to healthy tissue that carries the same target a treatment was built to recognise, so accurate recognition injures the tissue as well as the cancer.
records.summary:
On-target, off-tumour toxicity is injury from recognition of the intended target on healthy tissue. It differs from recognition of an unintended molecular target. The predictable, lymphoma-specific consequences of aiming at lineage antigens (B-cell aplasia, low immunoglobulin, and the effects of CD52, CCR4 and CD47 targeting) are described in the record on the cost of aiming at a lineage antigen, which this record does not repeat.

Many candidate cancer targets are normal proteins found at different levels or places in the body, so tumour-associated does not mean tumour-exclusive. A treatment that recognises its intended target wherever it is accessible, such as a chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell, can harm any healthy tissue that displays it, and tissue location, target density, receptor properties and exposure all shape the outcome. This differs from off-target cross-reactivity, in which the receptor recognises an unintended molecule, and from cytokine release syndrome, which is systemic inflammatory activation; the three can occur together. It also differs from payload toxicity in an antibody-drug conjugate: a pooled analysis of ADC trials found the key grade 3 to 4 toxicities grouped by payload and concluded they were likely off-target and related to the payload (Masters et al., 2018). Binding specificity is not tissue selectivity, and experience with an antibody against a target does not automatically carry over to a living cell with a different recognition and signalling system.

Two primary reports show the contrast. A patient with colon cancer metastatic to the lungs and liver received 10 billion autologous T cells expressing a trastuzumab-based CAR against ERBB2 (HER2), the largest number permitted in the first dose-escalation cohort, the day after a lymphodepleting regimen of cyclophosphamide (60 mg/kg daily for 2 days) and fludarabine (25 mg/m2 for 5 days). Within 15 minutes the patient had respiratory distress, chest imaging showed pulmonary oedema, and the patient died 5 days after treatment, with marked rises in interferon-gamma, GM-CSF, tumour necrosis factor-alpha, interleukin-6 and interleukin-10. At autopsy multiple organs showed systemic ischaemia and haemorrhagic microangiopathic injury and the lungs diffuse alveolar damage; histological examination of autopsy tissue found ERBB2 at 3+ in liver metastases and 2+ in lung metastases and much lower levels in normal lung parenchyma, normal liver and normal breast. The authors hypothesised that highly active ERBB2-directed T cells recognised ERBB2 on normal lung cells on first pass through the lung and released inflammatory cytokines that began a cascade ending in multiorgan failure; the autopsy findings were read as initial lung injury followed by days of hypotension and ischaemia, and the authors call the significance of the cells' reactivity against cultured primary cells unclear. This is a single case, with a stated dose and conditioning, whose mechanism is the authors' hypothesis and which gives no incidence for any CAR product (Morgan et al., 2010). In a trial of an affinity-enhanced T-cell receptor against HLA-A*01-restricted MAGE-A3 in myeloma and melanoma, the first two patients developed cardiogenic shock and died within days; no MAGE-A3 expression was detected in heart tissue at autopsy, and beating cardiomyocytes made from induced pluripotent stem cells triggered T-cell killing through recognition of an unrelated peptide from titin. That is off-target recognition of an unintended molecule, not the intended target in the wrong tissue (Linette et al., 2013).

How the question is asked before and during trials. FDA's CAR T-cell development guidance says to assess both undesired targeting of healthy tissue that expresses the intended antigen (on-target/off-tumour) and unintended targeting of other antigens, using examples such as tissue cross-reactivity studies with an antibody carrying the same recognition domain, protein arrays, cytotoxicity and cytokine-release testing on panels of primary cells, cell lines or stem-cell-derived organ systems, and relevant animal models, and encourages a combination of methods; antigen recognition domains can differ in affinity or avidity or recognise a different site, which should be evaluated, and CAR T cells can carry added components such as suicide genes. In practice a readout is a staining intensity or positive fraction, a binding profile, killing or cytokine release by healthy cells at a named time, and finally organ injury in the treated population; stained fixed tissue does not show a living organ's accessibility, an animal model may lack the human target, and a negative result in one panel is not a safety certificate. No universal expression cut-off is given here because no source read gives one. Whether affinity tuning, recognition logic or control switches improve safety for a particular design needs that design's own evidence. The 2026 ASTCT consensus abstract lists on-target, off-tumour toxicity among the toxicities for which it considered definitions and grading; its criteria were not readable.

notes: A fictional receptor kills X-positive tumour cells and normal airway cells that also display X: that is the on-target, off-tumour problem. If it also recognises Y on an X-negative healthy cell, that is off-target cross-reactivity. Binding or surface contact does not itself measure injury. Record tissue, assay sensitivity, staining intensity, positive fraction or calibrated molecules per cell, binding specificity, and healthy-cell killing or cytokine release at a named time; viable-cell tests consume the sample. Clinical organ injury is a further outcome in the actual population and regimen. A staining ratio, one negative panel or a control switch does not establish safety everywhere or guarantee reversal of an injury already present.

In a fictional tumour sample, 70 of 100 cells display an epitope accessible to the proposed receptor and 30 do not. A second target has only an RNA result, while healthy tissue was stained with a third antibody. Those measurements cannot rank safe receptor designs: ask for the actual binder’s recognition, the unrecognised tumour population and functional effects on relevant healthy cells. A more sensitive receptor might recognise additional tumour cells and additional healthy cells. Even a perfectly specific binder can harm healthy cells carrying its intended antigen; unintended binding to another molecule is a different failure. A sampled panel can miss antigen-negative cells, and an intracellular signal does not establish an accessible surface epitope. Repeat the relevant healthy-cell question under conditions, including inflammation, that could change recognition.

records.name: Dendritic-cell cross-presentation (cDC1)
records.tldr: Cross-presentation displays externally acquired protein fragments on class I HLA. Initial activation of a naive T cell is a further step called cross-priming.
records.summary:
Class I HLA commonly displays fragments of proteins made within the presenting cell. Cross-presentation means displaying externally acquired antigen on class I HLA. Naive CD8 T-cell priming is a further activation step requiring an appropriate presenting cell and supporting signals; tumour-cell display alone does not establish priming. The subset specialised for this is the type 1 conventional dendritic cell (cDC1): CD8alpha+ and CD103+ in mice, CD141 (BDCA-3)+ in humans, dependent on FLT3 ligand and the transcription factor BATF3 for development, internalising necrotic-cell material through CLEC9A (DNGR-1), a receptor for polymerised actin, and expressing the chemokine receptor XCR1, which favours contact with CD8 T cells (Alfaro et al., 2013).

The in vivo proof came from Batf3-deficient mice (Hildner et al., Science 2008): they lacked CD8alpha+ dendritic cells, their dendritic cells were defective in cross-presentation, and they failed to reject highly immunogenic syngeneic tumours. In mouse melanoma, CD103+ dendritic cells were the only antigen-presenting cells carrying intact antigen to lymph nodes and priming tumour-specific CD8 T cells, and they were required for PD-L1 blockade to work; expanding them with FLT3 ligand and activating them with intratumoral poly I:C improved responses to PD-L1 and BRAF inhibition (Salmon et al., Immunity 2016). This is why a scarcity of cDC1 in a tumour is read as one cause of a cold, checkpoint-resistant tumour, and why vaccine designs target antigen to cDC1 receptors such as CLEC9A, or expand and activate these cells, rather than relying on bulk monocyte-derived dendritic cells.

Cross-presentation names a display process, whereas cross-priming names the activation of naive CD8 T cells through it, which needs supporting signals and its own readout. Direct presentation remains possible: a dendritic cell that receives vaccine messenger RNA and makes the protein itself presents it directly. A cell can also acquire already assembled peptide-HLA complexes from another cell (cross-dressing), which does not show processing by the recipient (Wakim and Bevan, Nature 2011, PMID 21455179, mouse viral infection). External antigen on class II is not cross-presentation.

notes: The marker and mechanism list (CD141, FLT3 ligand, BATF3, CLEC9A as an F-actin receptor, XCR1) rests on the English abstract of Alfaro et al. 2013; the Hildner and Salmon findings rest on their abstracts. All three DOIs were resolved through Crossref and PubMed on 3 November 2026.
The checkpoint evidence cited is from mouse models; no human trial result is claimed here.
OnCo has no target records for XCR1, CLEC9A or BATF3 yet, so they are named in the text but not linked.

Follow the protein and the display molecule separately. In direct/endogenous presentation, the presenting cell makes the protein and uses its own class-I HLA. In cross-presentation, it acquires protein from another source, processes it and displays a fragment on its own HLA. In cross-dressing, it acquires an intact peptide-HLA complex from a donor surface, retaining the donor-associated display molecule. That starting point does not specify where the donor's peptide originally came from or how it was generated. This comparison tracks provenance, rather than one intracellular itinerary, physical transfer mechanism or activation outcome. Wakim and Bevan demonstrated transferred peptide-MHC complexes in a mouse viral model; this does not establish the same mechanism in every human setting.

Material uptake is not a display assay. Supplied peptide can load display molecules without demonstrating recipient processing of an external protein. Track donor and recipient HLA, the acquired material, target-specific display or responder results and suitable backgrounds. In a fictional experiment, a dendritic cell engulfs tumour debris and displays a tumour-derived class-I peptide; this supports cross-presentation. Without a naive T-cell activation measurement, cross-priming remains untested, as do downstream tumour killing and patient benefit. A cell marker alone cannot settle the question: in Jongbloed's defined human assays, both CD141-positive and CD1c-positive cells cross-presented soluble pp65, whereas only CD141-positive cells cross-presented the tested necrotic-cell antigen. The soluble-protein result also depended on stimulation conditions. These are antigen- and condition-specific findings, rather than a universal CD141 functional test.
